Constraint is non-negotiable: true error red is strictly for system/network error states, never for normal outcome states like `already covered` / complete / withdrawn.

I’m locking the screen graph with no added branching: session/auth gate, pod onboarding, relay board, request composer sheet, request detail sheet, receipt detail, profile, pod settings. No tabs, no third navigation stacks beyond shell+stack+sheets.

`AppGate` resolves to `AuthGate` when unsigned, to `PodOnboarding` when podless, otherwise to `RelayBoard` as default root. `RelayBoard` opens `RequestComposer` and `RequestDetail` via sheets; `RequestDetail` is the deep-link destination for push token wakeups. `Profile` and `PodSettings` are stack pushes from board header only. This keeps the IA aligned with your real workload: one core loop with two non-core surfaces.

For the core card state machine, we need explicit internal states, not shorthand labels: `openUnclaimed`, `awaitingConfirmation` (local tap in flight), `reconciling` (push wake + refetch path), `latchedConfirmed`, `latchedAlreadyCovered`, `reopened`, `stillOpen`, `withdrawn`, `completed`, `error`, and `queuedOffline`. That extra split between `awaitingConfirmation` and `reconciling` is the part you keep warning about, and it matters: if build agents collapse them, the loser-state proof looks wrong and the two-device demo loses trust. Both states share the same pulse visual language, but only `awaitingConfirmation` is your own action; `reconciling` is server-ack state propagation after background wake.

Offline must not fake confirmation: if action goes out while disconnected, the row is `queuedOffline` with chip “Queued — will send when connected,” never `awaitingConfirmation`, then transitions to `awaitingConfirmation` only once network actually starts the request. This is where your concern about draft semantics from `will send once connected` turns from policy into interface. Keep `queuedOffline` visually distinct and never remove state without confirmation.

Now screen-level behavior in concrete terms:

Auth gate states: signed-out empty/ready with Apple Sign-In CTA; signing in/loading with disabled UI and “Checking sign-in...” ; error has inline banner + retry; success routes by session token.
Pod onboarding states: no-pod empty has explicit pod-of-one CTA split between “Create pod” and “Join with invite code”; create/join in progress; invalid/expired code error; success routes only after server ack.
Relay board states:
- all-clear quiet state for pod-of-one: pod name, member count, “All clear” + note that no other members yet + “Share invite” action.
- all-clear populated pod state: same pod metadata with “No active requests” and single CTA “Post a pickup request”.
- active state: `BeaconCard` stack ordered by server-provided ordering; do not locally re-sort; show oldest/urgent-first as defined by backend.
- loading/error states with banner and retry, never blank.
Request composer states:
- editing, with note + urgency chip,
- `awaitingConfirmation` where action buttons are disabled,
- success only after backend ack,
- failed with retry and no optimistic outcome.
Request detail states:
- open/unclaimed with visible timer and accept CTA,
- `awaitingConfirmation` (local) and `reconciling` (remote refetch),
- winner latched confirmed and loser latched already-covered with identical transition timing and no red/alert styling,
- reopened and still-open escalation with timer/“Re-broadcast”,
- withdrawn (requester-only), completed (receipt available), action unavailable after completion.
Deep-link into request detail must have three branches: already synced (show immediately), sync-pending (spinner + “Loading request”), and no-longer-open/expired/withdrawn (specific message + close action, not generic error).
Receipt states: loading, loaded (internal + masked share projection), and unavailable fallback with reload action; placeholders for departed users are required (`Former member` style).

Every outcome-affecting action must remain persisted on server before UI state change is final. No toast/vanishing confirmation; states are always visible on card. This includes accept/release/complete/withdraw and no optimistic “saved/sent/confirmed.”

Secondary screens stay intentionally plain. Receipt, profile, pod settings share Theme tokens and spacing and semantic palette exactly; no custom transitions, no bespoke motion, no custom illustration. Receipt is the only exception worth extra typography density and hierarchy because it’s the external-share artifact, but it gets no extra animation.

Motion is fixed and shared:
open-to-awaiting uses calm heartbeat pulse scale 0.99→1.02 and border alpha oscillation with 0.9s easeInOut repeat; on resolution to either winner or loser, do the same 0.45s mechanical latch spring (response 0.45, damping 0.82). Loser and winner transitions are visually identical in timing and motion quality; only text/icon differ. Reduce Motion collapses both into quick crossfades (0.15s target) while keeping semantic text/icon change intact. Haptics are non-judgmental here: no “warning/error” vibration for loser; use soft/neutral success-like confirmation for both winner and loser only if you need a cue at all.

Accessibility has to be non-negotiable and explicit: icon-only controls need labels; card accessibility text should read as one sentence (`Request from {member}, status {status}, elapsed {time}, action available ...`) so screen reader users don’t have to parse multiple controls to understand state. No color-only state signaling; every state has icon+text. Min touch target 44x44. Respect Dynamic Type: allow chip and action stack to reflow vertically at AX3/AX5 (don’t clip/truncate). Enforce min spacing from spacing tokens so labels never overlap at any scaled size. Contrast must stay AA against semantic surfaces in both appearances.

I’m also making one explicit priority rule to protect the actual requirement: if time gets tight, you improve (1) open-to-awaiting pulse, (2) winner/loser latch, (3) completed/withdrawn terminal clarity, only then any polish on board resting and secondary surfaces.

If you want external Claude Design for handoff visuals, use this:
Create SwiftUI wireframes and high-fidelity mockups for pulse-relay in the Relay HUD language with Theme.swift tokenized exactly as specified (type scale, spacing, colors, radii above), with light and dark variants. Build screens: Auth Gate, Pod Onboarding (no-pod + create/join), Relay Board (all-clear + pod-of-one + active requests), Request Composer, Request Detail with full `awaitingConfirmation`/`reconciling`/winner/loser/withdrawn/stillOpen/complete/deep-link-expired states, Receipt, Profile, Pod Settings. Enforce no default List/Form/NavStack system chrome, no transient toast outcomes, zero outcome claims without server ack, and no chat/history/feed. Include BeaconCard and the exact pulse-to-latch motion (identical winner + loser) with Reduce Motion fallback, 44pt targets, no red for normal outcomes, and explicit loading/error/empty states for each screen.
No external design dependency is required to execute this; only use if you need a handoff pack before build.

**Claude (Frontend Engineer · Systems Thinker) — Round 2**

Codex, your spec is the more complete one and I think it should be the canonical base — the type scale, the spacing grid, the fourteen-component inventory, the navigation map, all of it is more fully worked out than what I threw down, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise just to defend my own numbers. But I want to push back hard on one specific thing in your palette before we lock it, because I don't think it's a stylistic quibble, I think it actually contradicts something the design_discussion phase already fought about and settled. Your neutrals — background `#F3F7FB`, surface.strong `#EAF0F7`, dark surface `#171E29` — all lean blue. That's exactly the "cold blue-black sci-fi/military HUD" register that got explicitly named and rejected in DEC-design_discussion-001, specifically because it makes the app read as alarming rather than calm-under-stress for a parent who's just realized they can't make pickup. Your state colors (the amber pulse, the teal confirmed) are fine and match what was locked — it's the neutral scaffolding underneath them that's quietly reintroducing the tone everyone agreed to avoid. I'd rather we warm those specific tokens — something like a warm off-white background instead of a blue-white, warm charcoal instead of blue-black for dark mode — while keeping everything else in your palette, your type scale, your spacing, and your radii exactly as you wrote them. This isn't me trying to win back my own hex values, it's flagging that we're about to ship a token file that technically satisfies "distinctive palette with light/dark hex" while quietly violating a decision that was actually argued over and locked two phases ago.

Second thing: your Relay Board active-state spec says cards are "sorted by urgency then age." I don't think we have an urgency field anywhere — go back through every decision from initial_discussion through app_features and there's no priority/severity/urgency tier on a request, just requester, note, and timestamps. If we write "urgency" into the formal spec without defining what it means or where it comes from, we're doing exactly the thing the phase rules explicitly forbid — "no adjective may stand in for a number" — and we're handing the build agent an undefined sort key it'll either invent arbitrarily or silently drop. I'd rather we just commit to what the data actually supports: sort by created-at ascending, oldest-and-therefore-most-aged request first, server-authoritative order, and the client renders it verbatim rather than re-sorting locally. That was my point from round one and I don't think anything in your spec actually disagrees with it, it just accidentally introduced a field that doesn't exist. If someone genuinely wants an urgency concept later, that's a real feature proposal for a future phase, not something to smuggle into a sort-order clause here.

Now the part I think matters most and where I want to be really explicit: your per-screen spec is thorough on states, but it's silent on how the client actually learns those states changed, and that silence is exactly where a build agent will take the shortcut that breaks the demo. Nothing in your spec says "don't trust the push payload" — and if that's not written down as an explicit rule, the fast, obvious implementation path for any competent iOS engineer is to decode the notification's userInfo dictionary and update the card directly from it, because that's less code than triggering a fetch. That's the bug I'm most worried about in this entire build, more than any color choice, because it would pass every screenshot review and even pass a casual demo, and then quietly fail the actual race-condition guarantee the whole app exists to prove, the first time APNs delivers two pushes out of order or drops one. I want this written into the spec as a hard architectural rule sitting alongside your interaction invariants: push notification arrival triggers an authoritative refetch of that specific request; the card only transitions after that fetch resolves; the payload itself is never rendered as state. And I want your Request Detail state list to explicitly carry the distinction I raised last round between "awaiting acceptance/accept ack" (this device's own action, mid-flight) and a second state for "I just learned the server already resolved this via someone else's action" — call it `reconciling` if you want a name for it — because if those two get collapsed into one internal case, the most likely implementation is that the losing device just snaps straight to "already covered" with no pulse at all, which kills the exact visual proof the two-phone demo is built around: both screens doing the same calm animation, one locking one way, one locking the other.

Same logic applies to two more states you didn't include that I don't think we can drop: `queuedOffline` for an action taken with no connection (visually and textually distinct from "awaiting confirmation" — one says "we're mid-round-trip right now," the other says "this hasn't left the device yet"), and a specific "this request is no longer open" state for a push deep-link that resolves to a request that's since been withdrawn or expired — that's going to happen constantly given how this app is actually used, someone taps a notification thirty seconds after the thing got handled, and if we don't name that state explicitly it'll get rendered as a generic error, which is scary and wrong for something that's actually a fine outcome. And since we're talking about relaunch behavior — R-018's force-quit-mid-accept test needs a home in this spec too. Cached data should render instantly on cold launch, per the local-first read rule everyone's agreed to, but it needs a subtle board-level "syncing" indicator — not per-card, a single top-level one — that persists until the first fresh fetch of that session actually lands, so a user who force-quit during a mid-flight accept doesn't see week-old cached state presented with the same confidence as fresh state.

Two small things and then I'll land on the Claude Design question. Your ElapsedTimerLabel spec says HH:MM:SS — I think that's the wrong format for what's actually a same-day, usually-sub-hour window; I'd rather it read MM:SS while under an hour and roll to "Xh Ym" past that, both because "00:14:32" is visually noisier in a small chip than it needs to be and because leading zeros on an hours field that's almost always zero is just wasted legibility. And I'd merge my ConnectionBanner idea into your SessionHintBanner rather than propose a separate component — but I want it explicit that the banner needs at least two distinct copy states under one component, "you're offline, your actions are queued" versus "connection's shaky, some pod members may not have gotten this yet," because those are different facts a user needs to act on differently and collapsing them into one vague "connection issue" string undermines the honest-delivery-count requirement we already locked as demo-critical.

On Claude Design: I said no external pass, you offered an optional prompt. I want to just close this instead of leaving two soft answers on the table — my actual reasoning is that the entire value of this design system lives in a state machine (the pulse, the latch, the parity between winner and loser), and a static mockup tool literally cannot represent that; the risk isn't "we don't have a design pass," it's "we get a gorgeous set of frames that can't prove the one thing this app is actually judged on, and someone mistakes polished statics for a validated interaction." So I'd lock it as: no external Claude Design pass for this build, we go straight from this spec into SwiftUI. I'd keep your prompt text on file as a fallback only, and only reach for it if a future iteration genuinely needs static marketing/App-Store-listing imagery, not as part of this build's design-to-code path.

These entries become the authoritative cross-phase DECISIONS LOG injected into every later phase, so completeness beats prose.

Talk like a person, not a report. The only fixed tokens are the `CONSENSUS: YES` / `CONSENSUS: NO` line and the `## Final Output` heading — everything else is natural English.
response:
This round did real work — Codex folded almost everything Claude flagged in round 1 (reconciling vs. awaiting-confirmation, queuedOffline, deep-link-expired) directly into the formal spec, kept the more complete token set and component/navigation architecture as the base, and locked the motion timing and priority order. That's good, substantive convergence and neither side is contesting it.

But Claude's round 2 response surfaces a few things that aren't settled yet, and one of them isn't cosmetic — it's a real contradiction worth stopping on. Codex's neutral palette (background `#F3F7FB`, dark surface `#171E29`, etc.) leans blue, and Claude points out this is the exact "cold blue-black sci-fi HUD" register that got explicitly named and rejected back in design_discussion (DEC-design_discussion-001) for making the app feel alarming instead of calm-under-stress. The state colors (amber/teal) are fine and match what was locked — it's specifically the neutral scaffolding underneath them that quietly reintroduces the rejected tone. Codex hasn't responded to this yet.

A few smaller but real loose ends: Codex's spec says board cards sort "by urgency then age," but there's no urgency field anywhere in the locked data model (just requester, note, timestamps) — Claude's right that this needs to become "server-authoritative created-at ascending, client renders verbatim," not an invented sort key. The "push payload is a wake-up signal, never rendered as state" rule is implied by the `reconciling` state Codex added, but hasn't actually been written down as its own explicit architectural rule yet. And three new, still-unconfirmed additions from Claude this round: a top-level (not per-card) "syncing" indicator for cold-launch/force-quit-mid-accept so stale cached state isn't shown with false confidence, a friendlier elapsed-timer format (MM:SS under an hour, "Xh Ym" past it, instead of HH:MM:SS), and splitting the connection banner into two distinct copy states (offline-queued vs. shaky-delivery) rather than one vague string. On Claude Design, Claude proposed closing it outright — no external pass for this build, keep the prompt on file only as a future fallback — but Codex hasn't confirmed that specific close yet.

CONSENSUS: NO

Next round: Codex needs to respond directly to the blue-neutral-palette objection (fix it or defend it against the earlier locked decision), drop "urgency" from the sort-order language in favor of server-authoritative created-at ordering, confirm the push-payload-never-trusted rule as explicit written spec text, and weigh in on the cold-start syncing indicator, the elapsed-timer format change, and the final call on external Claude Design.
